title: English Vocabulary 4 · Units 07–08
description: Advanced vocabulary on sales, markets, company negotiations, personality, workplace qualities, connotations and formality, including lexical contrasts and authentic usage patterns.
sourceNotice: Prepared as an independently written study package using the user-provided book to select learning targets. Original descriptions, translations, examples and usage notes do not copy textbook example passages or exercises.

audit.scope: Both teaching and exercise pages for Units 7 and 8, the buying and selling sections, full personality-characteristics chart, positive/negative connotation table, exercises 7.1–7.4 and 8.1–8.6, and corresponding answer keys.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is used selectively for individual words with well-established pronunciations; longer expressions and uncertain cases retain a blank IPA. Pronunciation differences are noted where relevant.
audit.languagePolicy: All learner-facing text is English except Brazilian Portuguese in pt. English unit names, categories, examples and notes are original.
audit.reviewMethod: Read and visually inspected both complete units, exercise pages and relevant answer key. Mapped primary targets and exercise-only additions, checked senses, preposition patterns, connotation, British English and natural Portuguese translations. Validated JSON schema, required types, IDs, field consistency, provenance and static TTS targets. No browser importer or live audio test was available.
audit.limitations: The supplied JSON includes no MP3 recordings; audio is empty. Structural linting does not establish browser compatibility, real spoken TTS output or speech-recognition accuracy. Some personality adjectives are context-dependent in evaluation.

units.title: Unit 07 — At work: careers
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 7. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Work and study · sales careers, buying and selling, company acquisitions
learningObjectives: Explain the differences between telesales, telemarketing, cold calling and hard-sell techniques.
Discuss purchasing power, brand loyalty, loss leaders and niche markets using natural collocations.
Describe buying decisions, auctions, trading up or down, and comparing value before purchase.
Distinguish takeover from merger and explain negotiations, capital assets and business start-ups.

sectionsChecked: A · A career in sales: annotated numbered expressions and selling terms
B · Buying and selling: purchase, stock, market and auction terminology
C · A career in business: numbered vocabulary, mergers, takeovers and agreements
Exercises 7.1–7.4 and Unit 7 answer key (PDF page 215)

items.example: She started in telesales before joining the company’s enterprise sales team.
items.note: Selling goods or services over the telephone; a job area, not a single sales call.

items.example: The retailer replaced indiscriminate telemarketing with opt-in customer campaigns.
items.note: Telephone-based marketing, not necessarily the act of closing a sale.

items.pt: ligações comerciais não solicitadas; prospecção por telefone sem contato prévio
items.example: Cold calling can damage trust when potential clients have not consented to contact.
items.note: Contacting prospective customers without any previous request or relationship.

items.example: Customers resisted the hard sell and asked for a straightforward comparison.
items.note: A pushy method of persuasion; often negatively evaluated.

items.example: Despite several rejected proposals, the founder persevered with her idea.
items.note: More formal than keep trying; often persevere with a task or persevere in doing something.

items.pt: abrir mão do seu dinheiro; gastar dinheiro, mesmo com relutância
items.example: People are unlikely to part with their money without a clear reason to trust the seller.
items.note: Part with expresses reluctant surrender of money or possessions.

items.pt: canal de televisão voltado à venda de produtos
items.example: The brand launched its new cookware range on a shopping channel.
items.note: A television channel selling items directly to viewers; here not a general shopping website.

items.example: The museum earns additional revenue from branded merchandise.
items.note: Goods intended for sale; generally an uncountable mass noun in this sense.

items.pt: mercado de produtos e serviços de lazer
items.example: The company entered the leisure market with affordable camping equipment.
items.note: A market segment related to hobbies, recreation and free-time activities.

items.example: After years in retail, she set up her own company selling outdoor equipment.
items.note: Set up means establish a business, not merely begin a new job.

items.pt: não parar de progredir depois de um sucesso inicial
items.example: He won his first major contract and never looked back.
items.note: Idiomatic: enjoy continued success following an important step; not about physical looking.

items.pt: poder de compra; capacidade de adquirir bens
items.example: Inflation reduced households’ purchasing power over the following year.
items.note: The financial ability to buy goods or services; not a formal decision-making authority.

items.pt: pesquisar preços e comparar diferentes fornecedores
items.example: Shop around before committing to a long-term internet contract.
items.note: Compare competing offers before buying; can be used beyond physical shops.

items.example: The cheapest service was not necessarily the best value.
items.note: Value measures what you receive for the price, not simply the lowest price.

items.pt: manter um produto em estoque; comercializar determinado item
items.example: Few local suppliers stock the replacement sensor.
items.note: Transitive stock means keep goods available for sale, not invest in shares.

items.example: The replacement batteries are finally back in stock.
items.note: For items held by a seller; contrast out of stock (unavailable).

items.pt: trocar por um modelo ou bem de maior valor
items.example: They traded up to a larger flat after their second child was born.
items.note: Replace an item, often a car or home, with a more expensive or higher-value one.

items.pt: trocar por um modelo ou bem de menor valor
items.example: To reduce their monthly expenses, they traded down to a smaller car.
items.note: Opposite of trade up; often prompted by a lower budget.

items.example: Reliable product reviews influenced her purchasing decision.
items.note: A decision whether and what to buy; the book links it to brand loyalty.

items.example: Despite the price increase, the manufacturer retained strong brand loyalty.
items.note: A customer’s tendency to keep choosing the same brand.

items.pt: produto vendido abaixo do custo para atrair consumidores
items.example: The supermarket used discounted milk as a loss leader to attract customers.
items.note: An item sold at a loss to encourage other, more profitable purchases.

items.pt: precificar um produto; estabelecer seu preço
items.example: A small business must price a product carefully to cover its costs.
items.note: Here price is a verb; distinguish it from the noun price.

items.pt: nicho de mercado; segmento especializado de consumidores
items.example: Specialised laboratory equipment serves a relatively small niche market.
items.note: A specific group of buyers with distinctive needs or interests.

items.example: The historic painting will go under the hammer next month.
items.note: Idiom for being sold at an auction; especially frequent in news and auction contexts.

items.example: The rare instrument attracted international bidders at the auction.
items.note: A public or online sale in which buyers compete by making bids.

items.pt: fazer um lance em um leilão; apresentar uma oferta
items.example: Several investors made a bid for the collection.
items.note: A bid is an offered price, particularly in auctions and competitive sales.

items.pt: autor do maior lance; maior ofertante
items.example: The artwork was sold to the highest bidder after a brief auction.
items.note: The buyer offering the greatest accepted amount at an auction.

items.pt: dominar um nicho ou mercado e reduzir a concorrência
items.example: The company cornered the market for bespoke cycling accessories.
items.note: Gain a strong or dominant position within a specific market.

items.example: Developing specialist software became a lucrative part of the business.
items.note: Usually suggests substantial financial returns; not just that a business avoids losses.

items.example: The start-up struggled with red tape before receiving its operating licence.
items.note: Uncountable idiom with a negative connotation about cumbersome procedures.

items.example: The project manager delegated routine administration to the operations team.
items.note: Organisation and management of business affairs; not automatically government bureaucracy.

items.example: The investors considered a proposition to acquire a minority stake.
items.note: A proposed business arrangement or offer; not a guarantee of an agreed deal.

items.pt: aquisição de controle; incorporação de uma empresa por outra
items.example: Staff were concerned about job security after the takeover.
items.note: One company gains control of another; compare merger, where two companies combine.

items.example: The merger created a single business with operations in several countries.
items.note: Two businesses combine; contrast a takeover that involves one controlling another.

items.pt: chegar a um meio-termo; alcançar um acordo com concessões
items.example: Both parties reached a compromise on the contract’s delivery schedule.
items.note: Each side makes concessions; reach, not keep, is the usual verb in this sense.

items.pt: negociar exaustivamente até fechar um acordo
items.example: The companies hammered out a deal after several weeks of talks.
items.note: Implies detailed negotiations to resolve disagreements.

items.pt: absorver ou incorporar uma empresa menor
items.example: The multinational swallowed up several regional competitors.
items.note: Metaphorical and sometimes critical: a larger business absorbs a smaller one.

items.pt: bens de capital; ativos fixos ou produtivos
items.example: The firm sold several capital assets to finance its expansion.
items.note: Assets held for a business’s operations or investment; context determines accounting classification.

items.pt: investir em um negócio ou empresa
items.example: She decided to invest in a business developing medical devices.
items.note: Use invest in a company, venture or asset; do not use invest on for this meaning.

items.example: The business start-up needed both funding and experienced staff.
items.note: Start-up is a young business; can also describe the process of starting one.

items.example: A local letting agency managed the property on behalf of its owner.
items.note: Especially British English for an agency arranging rentals, not property sales.

items.example: The lender wanted to see a realistic business plan before approving the loan.
items.note: A structured description of a business’s operations, market and finances.

units.title: Unit 08 — Describing people: positive and negative qualities
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 8. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: People and relationships · personality, positive and negative connotations
learningObjectives: Use nuanced adjectives to describe personality, temperament and professional behaviour.
Contrast favourable and unfavourable associations in near-synonyms such as shrewd/cunning and frugal/stingy.
Choose tactful descriptions according to register, including formal words such as parsimonious and garrulous.
Understand word families and conversational alternatives highlighted in the exercises and answer key.

sectionsChecked: A · Character and personality: labelled chart, personality adjectives and numbered meaning notes
B · Positive and negative associations: full contrast table
Exercises 8.1–8.6, especially connotation, word families and informal alternatives

items.example: Her imaginative approach turned a familiar problem into an original research project.
items.note: Positive creativity in forming ideas; not the same as imaginary (unreal).

items.example: The presenter was charming without seeming insincere.
items.note: Often positive social attractiveness, though it can also be used ironically.

items.example: A generous mentor shares credit with junior colleagues.
items.note: Positive willingness to give; the connotation differs from extravagant, which implies excess.

items.pt: pavio curto; que perde a paciência facilmente
items.example: He is quick-tempered but usually apologises soon after an argument.
items.note: Describes someone who becomes angry easily or suddenly.

items.pt: oportunista; que tira proveito das circunstâncias
items.example: The manager was criticised for opportunistic behaviour during the crisis.
items.note: Often disapproving: seeking personal advantage when an opportunity arises.

items.example: Her conservative approach to investment favours stability over risk.
items.note: Here about temperament and caution, not necessarily political affiliation.

items.example: His methodical troubleshooting identified the intermittent fault.
items.note: Positive systematic attention to steps and details.

items.example: The conscientious technician documented every calibration result.
items.note: Careful, responsible effort to do work properly.

items.example: His chauvinistic remarks offended several international colleagues.
items.note: Here excessive belief in one’s country’s superiority; the word can also mean sexist.

items.example: Even under pressure, she seemed a born leader who could unite the team.
items.note: Someone apparently naturally suited to leading others.

items.example: A sensitive supervisor can raise difficult issues without humiliating anyone.
items.note: Can mean considerate or easily affected emotionally, depending on context.

items.example: He became emotional when thanking the colleagues who had supported him.
items.note: Describes a strong emotional response; not automatically negative.

items.pt: se empolgar demais; perder a medida
items.example: We got carried away discussing possibilities and forgot the time.
items.note: Become excessively excited or absorbed; the reason may be positive or negative.

items.example: Her stubborn refusal to reconsider the schedule delayed the project.
items.note: Usually negative inflexibility; contrast resolute or determined.

items.example: The rebellious student challenged rules he believed were unfair.
items.note: Inclined to resist authority or accepted rules; context affects evaluation.

items.example: The journalist made a courageous decision to publish the evidence.
items.note: Positive willingness to act despite danger or fear.

items.example: She remained affectionate towards her family despite living abroad.
items.note: Shows warmth and fondness; typically affectionate towards or with someone.

items.example: The obliging receptionist found an accessible room for the visitor.
items.note: Willing to help or accommodate a request; stronger than simply polite.

items.pt: sentimental; emotivo por lembranças ou vínculos
items.example: He is sentimental about the notebooks he kept as a student.
items.note: Can convey warmth or excessive attachment to memories, depending on tone.

items.example: Her analysis was dismissed as superficial because it ignored key evidence.
items.note: For a person, suggests attention to appearances rather than substance.

items.example: Despite her expertise, she felt insecure about presenting in English.
items.note: Lacking confidence; not necessarily unsafe or physically at risk.

items.example: Their fun-loving flatmate organised weekend outings for everyone.
items.note: Enjoying leisure and social activities, often positive.

items.example: A perfectionist may find it difficult to delegate routine tasks.
items.note: A person who insists on extremely high standards; may be admirable or excessive.

items.example: The gifted musician mastered complex pieces at an early age.
items.note: Shows exceptional natural ability in a field; more than simply competent.

items.example: His tactless question embarrassed the new colleague.
items.note: Saying things without sufficient sensitivity; usually negative.

items.example: Her intuitive judgement helped her identify an overlooked risk.
items.note: Relies on instinct or immediate understanding rather than explicit analysis.

items.example: The stingy employer refused even minor workplace improvements.
items.note: Disapproving: unwilling to spend or give a reasonable amount; unlike thrifty.

items.example: The diligent researcher checked every result against the raw data.
items.note: Positive steady care and effort, especially with tasks and responsibilities.

items.example: An independent analyst can challenge the team’s assumptions.
items.note: Able or willing to act without relying excessively on others.

items.example: She remained placid during a heated discussion.
items.note: Positive emotional calm; can sometimes suggest a lack of energy.

items.example: His outgoing personality helped him build an international network.
items.note: Comfortable meeting people; does not mean leaving a place in this context.

items.example: It was selfish to take credit for the entire team’s work.
items.note: Prioritising your own interests without sufficient regard for others.

items.example: The cunning negotiator concealed a crucial condition until the end.
items.note: Often negative cleverness used for deception; compare positively evaluated shrewd.

items.pt: artístico; com talento ou sensibilidade para as artes
items.example: Her artistic instincts influenced the visual design of the exhibition.
items.note: Having ability or sensitivity related to art; distinct from artificial.

items.example: His over-anxious response made a minor setback seem catastrophic.
items.note: Over- marks excessive anxiety; often used for an over-anxious parent.

items.example: Her witty reply relieved the tension without belittling anyone.
items.note: Positive verbal cleverness and humour; compare terse or brusque, which are abrupt.

items.example: The host’s magnetic personality made newcomers feel included.
items.note: A strongly attractive presence that draws other people in.

items.pt: companhia agradável; pessoa com quem é bom conviver
items.example: I enjoy working with Marina because she is always good company.
items.note: Predicative expression: someone is good company; company is uncountable here.

items.example: After several broken promises, the investors became distrustful of management.
items.note: Inclined not to trust; often distrustful of someone or something.

items.example: The industrious apprentice volunteered for challenging assignments.
items.note: Positive persistent hard work, often slightly more formal than hard-working.

items.example: The shrewd investor recognised the risks before signing the agreement.
items.note: Often positive practical judgement; contrasts with negatively manipulative cunning.

items.pt: que dá apoio; compreensivo e encorajador
items.example: A supportive manager helped her develop confidence as a presenter.
items.note: Provides practical or emotional encouragement; often supportive of someone.

items.example: In an emergency, a decisive leader prevents unnecessary delays.
items.note: Able to reach decisions quickly and confidently; not necessarily authoritarian.

items.example: His extravagant spending left little money for essentials.
items.note: Often negative excess in spending, though it can also describe lavish design.

items.pt: pé no chão; prático e realista
items.example: Despite her success, the director remained down-to-earth and approachable.
items.note: Positive realism and practicality, without pretension.

items.example: Her altruistic decision prioritised patients over personal recognition.
items.note: Motivated by concern for others rather than self-interest.

items.example: He grew morose after weeks of disappointing negotiations.
items.note: More formal than gloomy; implies a persistently unhappy, withdrawn mood.

items.pt: de língua afiada; que faz críticas mordazes
items.example: The sharp-tongued commentator offended several guests.
items.note: Often describes people who speak in a harsh, critical manner.

items.pt: intelectual; interessado em ideias e raciocínio
items.example: The intellectual debate continued long after the lecture ended.
items.note: Can describe a person devoted to ideas or an activity involving reasoning.

items.example: A tolerant team welcomes constructive disagreement.
items.note: Accepting beliefs or behaviour different from one’s own; compare unprincipled.

items.example: It would be naive to assume that every supplier has the same priorities.
items.note: Lacking practical experience or scepticism; British English often writes naïve.

items.pt: materialista; excessivamente voltado a bens materiais
items.example: She disliked the materialistic attitude behind the advertising campaign.
items.note: Valuing money and possessions excessively, rather than relating to philosophical materialism.

items.example: The charity received unstinting support from local volunteers.
items.note: Positive and fairly formal for generous, wholehearted giving.

items.example: His immoderate demands made a settlement difficult.
items.note: Formal disapproval of behaviour or quantity exceeding reasonable limits.

items.example: The resolute campaigner refused to abandon the cause.
items.note: Positive firmness in purpose; compare stubborn, which implies unreasonable rigidity.

items.example: Through dogged investigation, the team located the source of the fault.
items.note: Positive perseverance despite repeated difficulties; typically dogged determination.

items.example: The obstinate committee rejected every proposed compromise.
items.note: Disapproving stubbornness, often stronger or more formal than stubborn.

items.pt: econômico; que administra bem o dinheiro
items.example: Her thrifty habits helped her save for further study.
items.note: Positive careful spending; contrast stingy (unreasonably unwilling to spend).

items.example: They maintained a frugal lifestyle even after their income increased.
items.note: Positive simple consumption and restraint, often in relation to lifestyle.

items.example: The parsimonious manager refused to replace essential worn-out equipment.
items.note: Formal and disapproving for extreme unwillingness to spend or give.

items.example: Her work-obsessed attitude left little time for friends or family.
items.note: Disapproving: a person focuses excessively on work.

items.pt: viciado em trabalho; pessoa que trabalha compulsivamente
items.example: He described himself as a workaholic until exhaustion forced him to rest.
items.note: Noun, often informal and negative; work-obsessed is adjectival.

items.example: The idealistic volunteers believed that fair access could transform education.
items.note: Positive dedication to ideals; may also imply impractical optimism.

items.example: She took a principled stand against misleading advertising.
items.note: Positive adherence to moral standards, not simply being strict.

items.example: His dogmatic approach discouraged reasonable disagreement.
items.note: Negative certainty that ignores alternative views.

items.pt: inflexível; indisposto a negociar ou mudar
items.example: An inflexible schedule created unnecessary difficulties for carers.
items.note: Reluctant or unable to change; may describe a person, rule or arrangement.

items.example: Her astute reading of the market saved the firm from a poor investment.
items.note: Often approving for accurate practical judgement; close to shrewd.

items.example: He gave a sly smile after concealing the final detail of the plan.
items.note: Typically negative or playful secrecy; unlike openly intelligent astute.

items.example: We need a sober assessment of the project’s risks.
items.note: Here means serious and restrained, not merely not drunk.

items.example: A serious adviser considers long-term consequences before recommending action.
items.note: Context may make seriousness positive, unlike morose or sullen.

items.example: The sullen teenager refused to explain why he was upset.
items.note: Negative silent resentment or bad mood; distinct from reserved or quiet.

items.pt: conciso e expressivo; sucinto e pertinente
items.example: Her pithy summary made the findings easy to remember.
items.note: Positive brevity that conveys meaning effectively; compare negatively abrupt terse.

items.example: The receptionist’s brusque reply surprised the visitor.
items.note: Abrupt manner that seems impolite; not simply concise.

items.example: His terse email gave no explanation for the decision.
items.note: Brief and often unfriendly; a terse reply contrasts with a pithy observation.

items.pt: de mente aberta; receptivo a novas perspectivas
items.example: An open-minded supervisor considers ideas from junior colleagues.
items.note: Positive readiness to examine unfamiliar views and evidence.

items.example: The unprincipled executive exploited loopholes to avoid responsibility.
items.note: Disapproving lack of moral standards; not the same as tolerant.

items.example: Unscrupulous traders misled customers about the product’s safety.
items.note: Strongly disapproving willingness to act dishonestly for advantage.

items.example: The chatty guide put the visitors at ease during the tour.
items.note: Usually positive or neutral informality; can be negative when talking is excessive.

items.example: His talkative nature made meetings lively but sometimes long.
items.note: Descriptive rather than necessarily critical; more neutral than garrulous.

items.pt: prolixo; excessivamente detalhado ao falar ou escrever
items.example: The verbose report buried the main recommendation in unnecessary detail.
items.note: Disapproving excessive words, especially in writing or formal speech.

items.example: A garrulous passenger kept telling stories throughout the journey.
items.note: Formal and often disapproving of a person who talks too much.

items.example: The unselfish volunteer shared the award with her entire team.
items.note: Everyday alternative to formal altruistic; the book asks for more informal synonyms.

items.example: His defiant response made it clear he would not obey the unfair order.
items.note: Everyday alternative mentioned in the answer key for rebellious; may be positive or negative.

items.example: After the failed trial, engineers remained wary of the proposed change.
items.note: Sceptical and cautious, often wary of something; less harsh than distrustful.

items.example: I was still green when I joined the research laboratory.
items.note: Informal figurative sense of lacking experience, not a reference to colour.

items.example: The accountant rejected a dodgy invoice with no supporting records.
items.note: Informal British adjective for unreliable or dishonest; also means precarious.
